projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Howard B. Hitchens was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Let's start with a little background. Subsequent to World War II I was drafted from college into WWII and served in the South Pacific. When the War ended I returned home and was demoted. So I went to Japan for a year and was in the Army of Occupation, with a good view of the Orient in WW II. Then I got out of the service in 1946, kept a Reserve Commission, finished college, received a bachelor's degree from the university and was recalled when the North Koreans invaded South Korea in 1951. I was with a B26 crew whose mission was interdiction, mostly night interdiction of supply lines, troops, etc. And that's what I was operating in as a navigator bombardier in October 1952 when we were hit and I had to bail out.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: You mentioned points in World War II?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: I don't remember specifics, but you were awarded a number of months you had served overseas for the number of medals and awards you received, combat operations, etc. I didn't have enough months when the war ended because I joined in the Spring of 1945 in New Guinea and then was at Nichols Field in the Philippines, then off to Okinawa on the Island where Ernie Pyle was killed, and that's where we were when the War ended. I recall vividly standing on the tarmac at the airfield at Southern Okinawa, probably 150 feet from General Mac Arthur and his staff as they were standing out there trying to make a decision to invade Japan. We had armed, equipped troops under an array of aircraft (C46's, etc.); this armada was to be used to put our troops and the armed troops were sleeping under the aircraft because we were under ready status. I was hiking around the Pacific having a good time! I was a navigator and was in Japan when the atomic bomb was dropped. I was a member of the Jolly Rogers (the 90th bomb group).

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Was there any cloud or any evidence?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: No, we were able to fly over the Nagasaki and Hiroshima bombings. We were up flying weather reconnaissance missions in our B24s and knew something was going on. We'd go up and fly for six to eight hours and I used to fly over Korea to the 38th parallel, on the west side, east across Korea, and it was on one of those missions we were able to fly over and see the devastation. It was incredible. It was almost this time of the year. It was August 12th and 15th when the two bombs dropped. Surrender was September 2.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: When were you discharged and what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: I was discharged in 1946, after a year in Japan, as a 2n Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: I stayed in the Reserve and when they went through the list of the people they needed for the Korean fracas, then my name came up and I was recalled in 1952. I had finished my graduate studies at Columbia and I was working menial jobs. The war was about a year old when I was recalled into the Air Force. The Air Force was separated from the Army in 1947.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Were you in Korea? -

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Yes, I was at Pusson. Kl and K2 designations for the airfields, and I flew out of Kl, at the tip of the Korean peninsula on a B-26. I had been an A-26 as an attack bomber in WWII. When the Air Force was created, they were redesignated and reinventoried. All bombers were Bs and all fighters were Fs and carriers were Cs.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: You said in 1952 you were shot down? -

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Yes, at the end of October on my 35th mission (flying 50 mission tours) and reported to 5th Air Force Headquarters as being eligible to go home when we had flown our 38th mission. It had taken that long to process the paperwork. I was on my 35th mission with a regular crew (a three man crew - pilot, navigator and bombardier and gunner (enlisted man)) and we made up the crew. My regular gunner and pilot were on R&R in Japan. I had volunteered to fly because it was autumn and I was hoping to get home for Christmas. I was flying with another pilot whose crew was on R&R in Japan. It was an interesting set of circumstances. The pilot I was flying with was probably the best pilot in our organization. He had been an American Airlines pilot and had hours and hours of flying time. He was our instructor pilot and did all the training and helped supervise all the training of pilots in the organization. We got into unfortunate circumstances. We were night flying on a bright moon-lit night, taking off at dusk. It took us about an hour to get up to North Korea into Pussan. We were working the main trunk rail lines that run north and south on the east coast of North Korea. We had thought we spotted a major train in a valley between two hills south of Han-Hung and made a run south from north to south and dropped a 500 pound bomb, creating a break in the rail line. We pulled up, came around and as we came around to the north again to make another run, we were in the valley and they were shooting anti-aircraft fire down on us. The 2n run was the fatal run because someone got a hit and our left engine caught fire and the pilot couldn't control it or get the fire out. We had fire dampening procedures on the aircraft. So we pulled up a little bit above the terrain that we were bombing and as soon as we saw the fire, Pete went to work with the firefighting system, which was unsuccessful, and the decision was to head south to southeast to the sea. As we turned east I called mayday and got contact with ground control, I don't know where. They put me in touch with a Marine winged aircraft that was flying top cover at about 20,000 feet for the purpose of providing assistance with navigation, etc. Told the Marine pilot where we were by grid coordinates and told him what our plan was. I looked back, was in the nose of the aircraft, and the flames were engulfing the whole left wingcell and it looked to me like they were getting into the cockpit. I called the pilot on the intercom and said "Pete, is it okay to bail?" and he said 'roger', and that's the last communication we had. I then hit the release arm on the trap door in the glass nose. I had a back parachute on and leaped forward; couldn't get myself backed up into the crawlway because I was too big to follow the recommended procedure, which is to tumble out headfirst, facing backward. I got panicky and leaped forward feet first and tried to protect my head. I got the cross-piece hooked on the bombsite head and I was hanging there half in and half out, then twisted myself around and fell free from the aircraft. I remember as I left the aircraft my last vision was the altimeter and we were at 900 feet above the ground. I tumbled once and thought to myself 'Do I wait to count to ten like they do in the movies, or do I pull the ripcord?" I pulled the ripcord and wasn't in the air very long, but the plane blew while I was in the air descending in the parachute. I turned myself around to the East and could see the plane exploding. I'm sure the other two guys didn't get out. I landed in a mud flat in the middle of the river and the mud flat had plants like cattails. I went through the procedure of assembling my parachute, getting it all together and trying to bury it. Everything I did automatically up until I got the parachute stuck into the mud and unbuckled the harness from me and discovered I had a dislocated shoulder and was bleeding from my hands and I then felt the shock settle in, which you always get in a situation like that. As the shock came, I began to do some silly thinking - like, I wanted to bargain my way out of the situation, so I got down on my knees and prayed "Look, if you just get me out of this, then I'll quit smoking." My options, I was logical enough for the most part - I could try to slip into the water (a current in the river) to the south of the flat I was on and try to float across and get into the marshes on the other bank that extended down to the south and hide that way; or slip into the water and try to avoid detection and float down - I had an inflatable Mae West on my body - to the sea where I could be picked up. Or I could stay where I was, hunker down and hope that I had not been seen. There was a full moon that night and I'm sure I had been seen. There was a small war going on all around me, with firing and shouting everywhere. I was sure I had been seen and elected to hunker down in the weeds and hope they wouldn't come looking for me. But that was to no avail. About 15 Korean troops assembled on the east end of the mud flat shoulder to shoulder and came walking to the west across the mud flat with guns at about waist level looking for me and I was crouched down. When they got to me, they just walked up on me and I just stood up and probably frightened them as much as they frightened me.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Above the 38th parallel?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Oh, yes. I was well up into North Korea. I could give you an idea on a map. They were so startled that it took them about 20 minutes before they realized I had a 45 caliber pistol in a shoulder holster and a clip of 8 shells. That was a part of my deliberation, also, whether I could get into a firefight and see what I could do with them. So they took the pistol away from me, got me into a little boat, and rowed across to the north bank of the river where there was a hard packed road. They walked me 1-2 miles to a village where I stayed (quite a curiosity). They kept me on a porch outside of a hut all night. The next day they sent a runner to find the tallest man in the region and made me stand up next to him. I was quite a bit taller then he was. I was quite a curiosity. The troops were, I believe, North Korean service troops. They were not regular fighting force. From there I spent 4-1/2 days travelling (walking mostly) through the hills and they walked me over to what they indicated was the foot of a tall mountain into a village. We got there at night. There are a couple of things I must tell you. What did I do about the dislocated shoulder? I had disabled it and was holding it to keep it from moving during the walking. I kept asking for a doctor but there was a language barrier. They brought a guy with a Red Cross armband on and he took a look at me at the shoulder and grabbed my arm and put his foot on my chest and he wrenched my arm around and popped the shoulder back. It set it myself and I've never had problems with it since. It was remarkable. At night I wound up at a village and I sat outside a hut while a tremendous negotiation went on. What transpired was that the Koreans were arguing with a Chinese Officer over control of me - what to do with me. I was completely ignorant of what was going on and was terrified. I figured that was the end of it and they would take me out and shoot me. I was completely surrounded by armed troops at all times. The Chinese officer gained control of me. He was a spectacular man - tall and thin and looked like Genghis Kahn, my images of him. He had a cold weather helmet with ear flaps, and a pony skin coat that was a swaggering image created by him. He had a retinue of two - one a driver and one an interpreter, who didn't know English, but knew Japanese and Chinese. He had a foreign motorcycle with a sidecar. The driver was on the motorcycle, the officer in the side car with the interpreter sitting behind him with his legs wrapped around the officer's waist. And they put me on the back of the motorcycle. We rode all night -- at least 6-7 hours on the motorcycle - to get to our next point where I was put on a truck. We were doing 20-25 mph on the motorcycle down these roads that had been bombed and we would hit holes and go sailing in the air. It was the wildest ride I ever had in my life. Then I was handed to Chinese control, put on a truck for a 3-4 day ride across Korea to the area east of Pyongyang (capital of N. Korea), which was a mining area. Came to be known as Pak's Palace POW Camp. I was kept isolated and saw no other prisoners. When I arrived in the mountainous mining area, a squad of Chinese troops stood guard over me all day and then did their regular labors on their off time. Frightening, but enlightening experience.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Could anyone speak English?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: No. Finally, I was put in a hut where an interrogator came. And that's when the misery started. They (there was a series of these people) spoke English. They threatened me with life and subjugation in Chinese and Korean and tried to keep me in a worried state, which wasn't hard to do. The interrogation was with the intent of getting me to sign a written confession that I had engaged in germ warfare. They hammered away at me for the rest of the three months that I was imprisoned until sometime in January. I was kept in solitary confinement and interrogated each day. They brought me food, which for the most part was rice, which I learned to love. Well I remember highlights of interrogation. I was able to argue a guy to a draw one day and he got angry with me and pulled out his pistol and fired a shot into the ceiling. He couldn't stand that. They kept me in very primitive conditions. Wouldn't allow me to go to the bathroom. At first I'd go in my pants, so I was in really miserable condition. They kept me in one position in the room that I was incarcerated over in this palace area. I had to stay in the Oriental squat. Could only lean up against the wall; the squat is bent at the knees and almost sitting on the ground. Christmas Eve came and they didn't feed me that day until almost dark came. A man came by and he brought about one half cup of red wine in wine bottle, roasted chestnuts and half dozen pieces of hard candy. He told me that even though they didn't believe in his Christian God, they were honoring his beliefs and would allow him to celebrate his holiday. I was able to drink that little bit of red wine, had 3 chestnuts and some candy and then I sat down and cried. One of the real low points in my experience. My interrogator at the time had a degree from Yale and was a very articulate Chinaman. I've learned since, through other people, that he was still alive a few years ago. A friend of mine had met and talked with him in China. When he got me to sign a confession after much tribulation, argument and resistance which finally wore down, I hand wrote a 2-page paper that was a complete fiction. I made up the information in it. I believe this was publicized and my name was released publically in the news media. My confession was published; I'm not sure of that, but believe it was. At the end of about those 30 days, they moved me down the hill to another little hut and I walked into this hut. It was quite dark in there. A Korean room ceiling is 5'9"; the Japanese style design with sliding paper doors and a paper ceiling. The hut was quite dark and standing in the room was a short Anglo guy that I could see. We looked each other quite awhile after they left me in the room with him. I didn't who I was facing. Finally we started talking. How did the Dodgers do last year; who won the pennant - checking each other out. Finally, George looked at me, stuck his hand out and said "Hi, I'm George Brooks, one of the big Pennsylvania mining guys you read about." And of course, I'm over 6 feet, so there was quite a disparity between us. I laughed and he laughed and we got on fine from then on. He was about 5'4", and had been a F51 fighter pilot. He suffered a concussion, fracture in his head and had some terrible times, but was in pretty good shape when I saw him - talking and talking. We stayed together about a month. Then they put us together into a truck with two other guys and drove us up to Yahoo River way up in North Korea near Manchuria. They put the four of us in a farm house complex. The other two guys were Paul Oakes from New Jersey, who had gone to Rutgers University, a great big guy, and Warren Lowe who was a broad- shouldered fellow. He played football for Purdue University and his father was a professor at Purdue. And the four of us got along. We tried to get George to team to play bridge; he was only one of the four who didn't know how to play, and he refused to do it. We made up cards out of old newspaper and made do.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Was it cold?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Yes, there were times when it was about 20 degrees below in that winter. They had given us the padded blue Chinese garb, just the standard stuff, and sneakers. And they gave us each a blanket. So we learned to cocoon when we slept at night. We would strip down (never sleep with your clothes on) to nothing and use your clothes to make a cocoon. The four of us would make one big pad at night when we'd be toasty and then freeze in the morning.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Could you go in and out?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: No, not without permission. The Korean farm is in a quadrangle. The house is one side, the storage sheds make another side, and the other two sides are fences. Each compound has some sort of a chopping block/tree stump where they grind grain, kill livestock. So the compound that we were kept in wasn't a nice farm compound. We were kept in the grain storage room with sacks of horse corn sitting in the corner and we would nibble on that when we were really hungry. We had our own forms of harassment. The Chinese guards were in the family farm house - the family was gone - and we were made to ask permission to go to the latrine. So you asked if you wanted to pee you shouted 'shobien' and number two was 'dabian'. So we would wait until we saw the guards relaxing and ready to light up a cigarette. Then we would ask for permission. The other really interesting thing was each day the four of us were each given a small wash basin full of hot water to be used for baths, ablutions in the morning and we even kept some of it to drink. We would pour some out into little cup containers for each of us; then brush our teeth; then wash and that was it. Warren and Paul, the big guys, decided they wanted to take harassment further. They would take the basin in the morning and would go out and set the basin on the stump on the courtyard, strip off to the waist, stand there and throw water on themselves, punch each other and rumble like bears. They did that for three days in a row and on the fourth day we looked out and they had their basin of water stripped to the waist washing themselves in zero degree weather.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Any contact with family?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: We were MIA's all the time. No one knew I was alive, but that's another part of the story. We were together for six weeks or so. After all these year's I've forgotten the details. We were together when Stalin died. One day all the guards showed up with black armbands, in the middle of March, I believe. I realized later that that's what it meant; that they were all mourning. We couldn't communicate with the Chinese guards very well because of all the dialects in the China. We were really hindered from communicating. It was very difficult. At the end of the period the four of us spent together we were split up again. I went into a period of 2-3 months of solitary confinement. It wasn't until the end of that period that I was moved in with a fellow named Bill Thornes, also an F51 pilot. All four prisoners were F51 pilots. He and I were taken to a little town - Chockton - and there was a large camp we passed that was a regular POW compound, where I could see many GI's, or what looked like American's, in this compound - camp 5 on the outskirts of Chockton. We were kept in a house in the little town together, Bill and I, and we finished the War together. We knew it was over mainly because we were sitting on a river across from Manchuria where the major MIG fighter base was. We used to hear the MIG fighters take off and land and occasionally watch dog fights between F86's and the MIGS from our hut. Anyway, on 27 July we woke up and there was dead silence. No aircraft sound anywhere. We looked at each other and said something's happening. That was the day they decided to end the war. Subsequently, we were taken to the schoolhouse, which was the community center in that town, and we were given a mock trial (a monkey trial). There was an officer and judges sitting at a table. They read off all the crimes we had committed and pronounced sentence on us. We were then taken into a little room, one by one, and there was an English-speaking officer there who read the terms of the Armistice. He asked us if we wanted to go home and be with the capitalist dogs or did we want to stay and fight for freedom with the peoples of the world. On the 2nd of September they fed us a magnificent meal of scrambled eggs and green peppers that I'll never forget. It was the greatest feast I had there. It was unbelievable. There was hot tea, and then we were loaded on trucks and taken to Kaesong where we were given haircuts and prepared us for repatriation. I was repatriated in the last truckload out of North Korea on September 6, 1953. People with me in that truck were a B29 crew who had been kept in Manchuria for the whole War. It was an extremely emotional experience. We cried and cried on being repatriated. One of the anecdotes - my wife had great faith that I was alive. I don't know why. She had no evidence, no reason to believe I was alive. She sat down and wrote me a one-page letter every day that I was gone and she would address it to Lt. Hitchens, North Korea, put a stamp on it and put it in the mail. She never got one of them back. When they processed us - that was a joint processing operation with the Red Cross and our military to process - the first thing they did when they got you out of communist hands was to get you out of the bug-ridden clothes, delouse you and give you a good hot shower and give you a robe and slippers and put you in your own hospital bed. Part of the processing included a mail call. I stood behind this little desk and said "you've got to be crazy, I don't have any mail". And he said, 'well let me take a look.' And he came back with two letters that Midge had written. Mind you she was 8-1/2 months pregnant when I was shot down. She was due in November and I was shot down at the end of October 1952. And I had in my ramblings imagined that she had collapsed and died of grief when they told her I was missing. Had no idea what happened. The first letter was very innocuous; the 2nd letter was very powerful. She gave me a weather report and said I am fine, Skip is fine and John is just too wonderful for words. And I knew I had a son.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Your first child?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: No, my 2nd. We had agreed on names before we were married. He was 10 months old when I got home. That was a remarkable event. I don't have the letters anymore, so I don't have the dates. I believe they were written close to my repatriation. I have virtually nothing left of that experience, because I wanted to get rid of every vestige of it because it was a tough time. I have a little teaspoon that a guard gave me mid-way through my captivity because I was having trouble with chopsticks. I kept it all the rest of my captivity and brought it home with me. And I still have that. It's worn down some.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: How much time were you in solitary?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: About half of the time. The first three months and then the 3rd three months of the approximate year. I used to know exactly which dates, but I've forgotten. The healthiest thing that happened to me was that my commander, when I came back to the United States - oh, footnote, the Air Force policy was the only reward I got out of being a prisoner was that I could have my choice of any assignment that was feasible. So I elected to be a navigation teacher and I was assigned to Mather Air Force base, Sacramento, CA. My commander then Col Sam Maddox who became a LTG in the Air Force, when I arrived at the base the first thing he did was to interview me. He said we had some public relations problems and I was going on the 'chicken and peas' circuit. He sent me out and I spoke to every Kiwanis Club, Rotary Club and service club in northern California. And it was the most wonderful thing for me because it allowed me to take that story out of me and put it out there on the table for other people. I had it down - a 12 minute, 20 minute, 45 minute and 90 minute pitch. Just tell me what you want. And I had a great time with that. I didn't much like the luncheons but the people were wonderful. Really the most healing thing that happened to me. And Sam Maddox went on to become the head of the training command in the U.S. Air Force. A wonderful man.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: How did you keep your sanity while in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: It wasn't easy. I learned that there were prison camps with a set of people who react to a situation where they have to do something - with their hands. If you go to POW museum and look at their products, you'll see clocks, embroidery and other handiwork and crafts to keep busy. Then the other people stay in their heads. I stayed in my head and imagined. Eventually I composed in my head, built a vacation cabin and figured out how much lumber, nails, screws, etc. It was a wonderful preoccupation and I did that over several months period. There were days when I didn't know whether this was in the worst solitary confinement periods when I didn't know if it was day or night and would sneak over to a crack in the door to check to seek reality. It worked! I don't know whether I'm proud of that or not. But I did survive and I went on to academic studies with a PhD and a lot of different things in my life. I have a lot of self confidence.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: What did you learn or benefit from these experiences?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: Well, I learned a wealth of things. One of the basic reasons is we people on the earth are all alike. I was able one day to have a conversation with a Chinese guard and he indicated he had two children at home and was worried about them. That was a very telling moment in my captivity. People are alike and to think we are different is crazy. We aren't. We appear different. I can remember during World War II seeing my first Japanese prisoners and I was so full of hatred that I wanted to take my pistol out and shoot them. But they were just my fellow man. We were right to hate them to get through the War, but that was my big lesson out of Korea. I stayed in the Air Force after Korea and retired in 1969. The Air Force sent me to Syracuse University. I was a member of the original faculty and staff at the Air Force Academy in Colorado. That was a very exciting time in my career and in the Air Force. The Academy, because it had priority, was able to get all the bright people you could think of in the Air Force assembled at the Academy. It was such great fun to be there. I can remember the interminable arguments we had in putting a curriculum together deciding what an air force officer should know. We argued by the hours and hours and there were formal arguments. Professors voted on these issues. We were not just another West Point or Annapolis. Our slogan said "We proceed unhampered by tradition". One of the funniest things cadets did at the Air Force Academy was they created a mythical cadet. His name was Nino Baldacchi.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: What did you teach?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: I went there to teach English, but they tapped me to set up an educational television and communication system. I developed audio visual services at the time, which came to change into instructional technology. We put in a very elaborate television system at the academy, which was my responsibility. I had 13 illustrators who worked full time in the art shop, woodworking, sheet metal shop, plastic shop. So that's what I did for my whole time there. This coincided with a revolution occurring in American education that we needed people to worry about including television, radio in the curriculum. My degree was in that field a Ph.D. in instructional communication. The first one in the Defense Department to receive one. Wound up as a consultant to the other academies.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Did you keep in touch with your fellow POWs after you returned?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: No. Immediately after we returned, a month of two, four of us who played cards gathered in New York and had dinner at Mama Leone's and that's the last time I've seen or talked to any of them. I tried to locate Paul Oakes and sent the blind message through Department of Defense, but he has never responded. Perhaps he doesn't want to be in communication. The last I heard was that he flew choppers in Vietnam. I Don't know what happened to Brookes. Bill Thornes is active with a Korean organization and is active with a POW museum established as a national museum at site of Andersonville Prison, Georgia. I've talked to him on the phone a few times. I'm a member of more organizations then I want to be a member of: ex-POWs, Military Officers of America; Veteran's of Foreigh Wars and Purple Heart Organization. There are no medals of any great significance, just the Air Medal from World War II and Korea, and meritorious service for service at Air Force Academy. Most of them are just service awards.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Anything else you'd like to say?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: One thing I would like to say. I'm living in the age of John McCain and his dominance of the media. And he was a POW in Vietnam in the Hanoi Hilton. The Korean War people preceded you, John, and we learned a hell of a lot we tried to convey to subsequent service members. President Eisenhower promulgated the code of conduct in August 1954 well after the Korean War was over. That code was put together based in large part on experiences of people like myself. There's nothing heroic about being a prisoner. We're just unlucky and if you survive, you're lucky.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: How many are still over there that you know of?

sp.speaker: Howard B. Hitchens
sp.p: None. That's a phenomenon that occurred well after Korea. For the Vietnam war those concerns have arisen and there were a lot of people who perished and we don't know what happened to them or didn't perish. John Kerry put a lot of that to rest. He and McCain went over and spent months researching that and putting the effort into determining if there were any numbers left and they couldn't find any. We're getting remains back, but so far as I know there was never anybody. I was observant. I remember there was an English...see Korea was a United Nations War so we had South African troops, British troops, there and it was a really mixed bag of troops. And there was a colonel who was imprisoned sort of down the street from where I was just before the war ended before the armistice in 1953. We used to hear him; he was absolutely resistant to any interrogation and only gave name, rank and serial number. They kept him shackled in chains; we could hear the chains. And this one night shortly before the armistice we were awakened by a disturbance of chains rattling with him apparently trying to escape. Then we heard a shot fired and he perished. He probably said I've had enough. And you do reach that. There are guys who are unable to cope with it mentally and did go straight to institutions from their experience. There were 50 flyers captured in Korea who came back. There may have been some who perished. Most of us met each other. I came home on ship out of Inchon when I was repatriated and the ship was loaded with repatriated soldiers from operation big switch. COL Walker McKeown, Commander of 4th Fighter Wing. He signed a manufactured confession as I had done and he was not allowed to continue his Air Force career when he returned home. He shot down 27 airplanes in World War II, and was one of the greatest pilots.

sp.speaker: Dorothy Brault
sp.p: Thank you for this wonderful interview and your years of service.
